speaker: Elena Verna
title: 10 growth tactics that never work | Elena Verna (Amplitude, Miro, Dropbox, SurveyMonkey)
question: In SaaS marketing, why does redesigning a company's homepage or doing a rebrand rarely increase user acquisition at launch?
guest: Never once have I seen a rebrand or redesign, especially of your key marketing site, produce good performance results at launch. There are valid reasons to rebrand or redesign—like entering a new market or category, or updating after your product has evolved—but those are a lagging indicator that something needs to change. It's a new starting point, and that starting point is going to be much lower than your current experience because your old site has gone through some level of optimization, whereas a rebrand is always a shot in the dark. It might be prettier, sure, but that doesn't mean it performs well. The best I've ever seen is net-neutral results that give you a better ability to optimize toward a higher global maxima. So if you do one, forecast for an initial hit and bake in three to six months of optimization work after launch to bring it back and outperform—which is what most teams forget to do because they move on to the next project right after launch.

points.core: A redesign replaces an already optimized site with an untested lower-performing baseline.
points.note: Accept: overhauling the marketing site wipes out accumulated prior optimizations and launches as a shot in the dark that typically dips conversion or at best lands net-neutral, regardless of visual polish. Do not credit: claims that a modern or cleaner design naturally lifts acquisition.

points.core: A rebrand raises the long-term optimization ceiling rather than lifting immediate launch metrics.
points.note: Accept: valid rebrands respond to product or market evolution to unlock a higher global maxima later, not immediate seven-day launch acquisition gains. Do not credit: generic branding advice without distinguishing long-term ceiling from launch performance.

points.core: Beating the previous baseline requires budgeting three to six months of post-launch optimization.
points.note: Accept: teams must forecast an initial performance dip and dedicate months (e.g., 2-6 months) of post-launch iteration to recover and outperform, rather than moving on right after launch. Do not credit: vague advice to monitor metrics without budgeting sustained post-launch optimization.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
A redesign or rebrand rarely lifts acquisition at launch because it changes how the company looks, not how many people show up or why they would buy.

Acquisition is driven mainly by upstream factors: traffic volume and quality from channels like search, referrals, paid ads and word of mouth, plus the product's underlying value, pricing and market fit. A new homepage or logo doesn't create new demand or new distribution; the same visitors arrive with the same intent.

Several things can actually make launch numbers flat or worse. Big-bang redesigns bundle many untested changes, so improvements and regressions cancel out, and you can't tell which is which. They often discard copy and flows that had been incrementally optimized. Returning visitors face unfamiliarity, and changed URLs, content or domain names can temporarily hurt SEO rankings. Rebrands also reset accumulated brand recognition.

Finally, these projects tend to be driven by internal motives (aesthetic fatigue, new leadership, repositioning) rather than by evidence of a customer conversion problem. Any benefits, such as clearer positioning, moving upmarket or brand trust, accrue slowly over months, not on launch day.

points.why: The response links flat or worse launch performance to replacing incrementally optimized copy and flows with untested changes.

They often discard copy and flows that had been incrementally optimized.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Redesigning a SaaS homepage or launching a rebrand rarely boosts user acquisition immediately because neither creates new distribution or top-of-funnel demand; at best, they only influence conversion rates on existing traffic. Worse, sweeping overhauls change dozens of variables simultaneously—layout, navigation, calls to action, and copy—wiping out hard-earned, incremental conversion optimizations and introducing untested friction without isolating what actually drives signups.

Internally driven rebrands also frequently replace clear, problem-focused value propositions that buyers immediately understand with abstract, aspirational messaging crafted to satisfy executives and investors rather than prospects. Meanwhile, structural URL changes and rewritten copy often disrupt organic search rankings, while unfamiliar visuals temporarily weaken recognition across paid ads and word-of-mouth referrals. Because aesthetics rarely solve underlying positioning or channel bottlenecks, acquisition typically stays flat or dips at launch, improving only after teams iteratively test the new baseline against real user behavior.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A homepage redesign or rebrand rarely increases acquisition at launch because it changes how you present yourself to people who already find you. It doesn't create new demand or new traffic. The homepage sits in the middle of the funnel. It converts visitors who arrive through other channels like search, referrals, ads, word of mouth, and product virality. If those channels stay the same, the number of prospects stays roughly the same, and a nicer page can only slightly improve the conversion rate on that fixed traffic.

The launch announcement mostly reaches people who already know you, such as customers, followers, and subscribers. They aren't new users. Prospects don't care about your visual identity. They care whether you solve their problem, and the redesign usually doesn't change that.

Redesigns can also hurt in the short term. They may disrupt SEO through changed URLs and content, remove copy that was already converting well, or confuse returning visitors. They're also rarely A/B tested, so any gain is hard to see or prove.

Acquisition grows from distribution and product changes: new channels, better positioning aimed at specific segments, pricing, and features worth talking about. A cosmetic refresh doesn't provide those.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: A homepage redesign or rebrand rarely increases user acquisition at launch because it changes presentation rather than distribution. Most SaaS companies are constrained by how many qualified buyers discover them through search, referrals, content, or paid channels, and a new visual identity does not immediately generate more traffic. In fact, launches frequently depress acquisition at first: redesigns often replace battle-tested messaging and conversion paths with unproven layouts, while structural or copy changes can temporarily disrupt SEO rankings. Rebrands also reset hard-won brand recognition, creating friction for returning visitors and word-of-mouth referrals who no longer recognize the name or look. More fundamentally, SaaS buyers convert because they quickly grasp how a product solves an urgent problem, trust its social proof, and see a low-friction path to value—not because of fresh aesthetics. While a thoughtful rebrand can eventually support stronger positioning and higher conversion rates, those gains compound slowly through sustained messaging and channel execution rather than appearing on launch day.

points.why: The response links the initial acquisition dip to replacing proven conversion paths with an untested design.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A homepage redesign or rebrand changes what people see when they encounter the company. It rarely changes how many qualified buyers encounter it at launch. If search rankings, ad spend, referrals, and sales outreach stay roughly the same, the company is still reaching much the same audience.

A redesign can convert more of that audience if it fixes a specific problem, such as an unclear value proposition or a confusing signup flow. But a visual refresh alone gives buyers little new reason to act. A rebrand can build recognition and trust over time through repeated exposure. If acquisition spikes at launch, it’s worth looking at what else shipped alongside it, such as a campaign, a product announcement, or a new offer.

points.why: The response attributes flat launch acquisition to unchanged audience reach and never explains how a redesign replaces an optimized site with an untested baseline that typically converts worse.
The response describes recognition and trust building over time but does not explain how a rebrand creates room for future optimization to surpass the old site's performance.
The response neither forecasts an initial performance dip nor calls for budgeting several months of post-launch iteration to recover and exceed the prior baseline.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
A homepage redesign or rebrand changes what people see once they encounter the company. On launch day, it usually reaches people who already know the product. If the same channels bring in roughly the same visitors, signups will rise only if the new homepage persuades more of those visitors to try it. That can happen when the old page made it hard to understand who the product was for or why it was worth trying. A visual refresh alone rarely solves that problem.

A rebrand can still help acquisition over time. As prospects encounter the new identity across campaigns, recommendations, and the product itself, they may be more likely to remember the company when they need it. That recognition takes repeated exposure to build.

points.why: The response explains how traffic and persuasion affect signups but never identifies the loss of accumulated optimizations when an untested homepage replaces the old one.
The response attributes long-term acquisition gains to recognition from repeated exposure, leaving the higher ceiling for future optimization unaddressed.
The response neither forecasts a launch dip nor calls for months of post-launch iteration to recover and surpass the previous baseline.
